The arc is a textbook rehabilitation story, and management never lost the thread.

The most telling shift is linguistic: management moved from talking about *defending* the franchise to *leveraging* it for market share, explicitly tying a hoped-for rating upgrade to future share gains — "when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow" (Q4 2025). Management treats it almost as housekeeping; it is real, durable value.

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** This is a competently-run, conservatively-financed reinsurer that has rebuilt its earnings and capital base with unusual discipline, beaten its own guidance every quarter, and just cleared its largest legal overhang at a pre-provisioned cost.

# SCOR SE (SCR.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from eight consecutive earnings calls (Q4 2024 through Q4 2025) cross-referenced against the hard financials.*

SCOR is France's global reinsurer — the world's fifth-largest — selling reinsurance (insurance bought by insurance companies) across property-and-casualty (P&C), life-and-health (L&H), and running a large, high-quality bond portfolio on the side. The story across these calls is a clean, methodical turnaround: a company that took a brutal write-down in 2024, rebuilt its credibility quarter by quarter, and finished 2025 with the highest annual profit in its history.

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The arc is a textbook rehabilitation story, and management never lost the thread.

The starting point (Q4 2024, reported March 2025) was damage control. The headline was a near-zero full-year result — net income of just €4 million for fiscal 2024 — caused by a deep life-and-health "assumption review" (management re-checking the long-term assumptions behind its life book and finding them too optimistic). CEO Thierry Leger's framing was: the underlying businesses are strong, the reported number is a one-off. He leaned hard on the adjusted figure — "our full year net income for the group would be €728 million, translating into a 14.9% ROE" (Q4 2024) — and on a fully-absorbed solvency ratio of 210%.

From there, each quarter added a brick. Q1 2025: an 18.3% return on equity and a combined ratio (claims plus expenses divided by premiums; under 100% means underwriting profit) of 85%, beating the company's own "below 87%" target even after absorbing €140 million of Los Angeles wildfire losses. Q2 2025: 22.6% ROE, an 82.5% combined ratio, economic value growth of 10.5%. Q3 2025: 21.5% ROE, an 80.9% combined ratio. Q4 2025 (reported March 2026): the capstone — full-year net income of €846 million, "the highest level in SCOR's history," 19.1% ROE, solvency at 215%, and a dividend raised to €1.9.

The growth drivers shifted in an honest, disciplined way. P&C deliberately *shrank* the riskiest line (U.S. casualty) and grew "diversifying" lines (alternative solutions, engineering, marine, longevity). Life-and-health pivoted from low-margin mortality protection toward longevity and financial solutions — management openly warned this would dent new-business volumes first ("a kind of J curve," Q1 2025) before the higher-margin mix showed up. Nothing was quietly dropped; the few disappointments (revenue misses in Q2 2025) were named and explained.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

This is where SCOR scores well: the narrative is, if anything, *poorer* than the numbers justify — management under-promised.

| Management claim | The hard number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Highest net income in SCOR's history… 19.1% ROE" (Q4 2025) | Fiscal 2025 net income €851M (screener) / €846M (mgmt), EPS €4.76, up from €4M / €0.022 in 2024 | **Matches.** A genuine, dramatic recovery — though off a near-zero base, so the "+21,536% EPS growth" is an arithmetic artifact, not real momentum. |
| "Combined ratio below 87%… excellent P&C performance quarter after quarter" | Gross margin 94.3% (stable); the combined-ratio run (85% → 82.5% → 80.9% → strong Q4) is consistent | **Matches.** Underwriting discipline is real and verifiable across all four quarters. |
| "Economic value growth of 13.7%… solvency 215%" | Net cash position of €17.99B (recomputed: €21.55B cash vs €3.57B debt); P/FCF just 5.2x | **Matches and then some.** The balance sheet is genuinely fortress-like. |
| Returns are strong (ROE ~19%) | But ROE on the screener reads **2.3%** and ROIC **0.3%** | **Diverges — a measurement gap.** The screener's trailing returns are still dragged by the 2024 write-down year; management's 19% is the clean run-rate. The truth is in between, but the *trajectory* favors management. |
| Revenue "flat… growing in a profitable and diversified way" | Revenue actually *fell*: -5.4% in 2025, a -3.4% three-year trend (€16.4B in 2022 → €14.8B in 2025) | **The honest blemish.** Top line is shrinking, partly by design (exiting U.S. casualty, a large contract commutation), but it is shrinking. This is a profitability-and-capital story, not a growth story. |

The cleanest tell of credibility: in Q4 2024 the CFO told an analyst the €728M adjusted figure is "adjusted of everything. So it's clean and it's a good base for your estimates" — and 2025 delivered €846M, *above* that base. They beat their own clean baseline.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Rising, then settling into earned confidence.**

- Q4 2024: defensive but composed — "following a very challenging year," heavy emphasis on resilience and absorption.
- Q1 2025: "I'm satisfied… a good start into the year," still hedged ("There is still work to be done").
- Q2 2025: "very satisfied with the level and the quality of the results."
- Q3 2025: a notable shift to offense — Leger volunteered an unprompted lecture on cycle discipline ("I have seen this before. This is the time when wrong strategic decisions can have a detrimental impact"), the posture of a CEO confident enough to coach the market rather than defend himself.
- Q4 2025: outright pride — "finishing 2025 on a high note… the highest level in SCOR's history."

The language migrated from defensive (absorption, resilience, one-offs) to offensive (franchise, market share, "leave no stone unturned to find profitable opportunities"). Guidance got *more*, not less, specific over time.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.** This is a sandbagging pattern, the good kind. Every quarter the combined ratio came in well below the "below 87%" guide (85% / 82.5% / 80.9%), and management repeatedly declined to lower the guide despite being asked directly — "we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence" (Q1 2025). The screener's earnings-beat rate of 6 of 7 quarters (86%) corroborates the transcript impression exactly. ## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Three recurring pressure points, handled with varying candor:

1. **The Covéa arbitration.** Analysts (Huttner, Q1 2025) repeatedly probed the provision tied to a dispute with French insurer Covéa over life retrocession treaties. 2. **FX hitting solvency.** Analysts (Shuck, Q2 2025) pushed on why a weak dollar dented solvency more than the published sensitivities implied. The CFO's answer was genuinely murky ("we still need to work… to refine… the way we compute the sensitivities") — a real, if second-order, soft spot.
3. **Revenue growth / the 4-6% P&C target.** Pushed repeatedly (Hardcastle, Q3 2025), management effectively abandoned the 4-6% revenue CAGR as a hard target, reframing it as "an outcome, not an objective." 🟢 Combined ratio beating guidance every single quarter while *building* reserve buffers — they hit the 2024-2026 buffer target two years early and kept adding. Hidden earnings power.
🟢 Fortress balance sheet: solvency 210% rising to 215%, a net cash position near €18B, an A-rated, short-duration bond book earning rising reinvestment yields (3.5% regular income).
🟢 Dividend raised to €1.9 with an explicit "ratchet" floor — a credible, growing income signal.

🔴 The 2024 life-and-health write-down is recent history, not ancient — management itself says it takes "at least 2 years" to validate the new assumptions, so the all-clear is not yet earned.
🔴 An ongoing French criminal examination tied to the late former chairman Denis Kessler lingers in the background (no direct company implication claimed, but unresolved).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The most telling shift is linguistic: management moved from talking about *defending* the franchise to *leveraging* it for market share, explicitly tying a hoped-for rating upgrade to future share gains — "when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow" (Q4 2025). One of five rating agencies had already moved positive, with management expecting "others will follow in the next 12, 18 months."

A quieter signal: the tax restructuring (repatriating profit to France, redomiciling an Irish platform to Paris) is a multi-year, low-glamour value lever that should pull the effective tax rate toward 28% and below, and unlock ~€250M of currently-unrecognized deferred tax assets. Management treats it almost as housekeeping; it is real, durable value.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STRENGTHENING.** This is a competently-run, conservatively-financed reinsurer that has rebuilt its earnings and capital base with unusual discipline, beaten its own guidance every quarter, and just cleared its largest legal overhang at a pre-provisioned cost.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** this is a *quality-and-capital* story, not a catalyst story — and the one true catalyst (the Covéa ruling) has already fired, with the stock essentially unmoved at ~€31. The director must decide whether a cheap (5.2x price-to-free-cash-flow), well-capitalized, no-growth reinsurer trading slightly *above* its conservative Buffett/EPV fair value is worth capital when the re-rating trigger is spent and the top line is flat-to-shrinking.

**Moat assessment.** SCOR's moat is a regulatory-license-plus-scale franchise (a "Tier 1" reinsurer with global licensing and diversification that smaller players cannot replicate) reinforced by intangible reputation with cedents. It is genuine but **narrow** — reinsurance is a capital commodity where pricing is set by the cycle, not by any single firm, and SCOR is the smallest of the global majors. Crucially, the moat is **widening**, not eroding: combined ratios are improving (85% → 80.9%), reserve buffers are growing, and the clean-year ROE (~19%) sits well above the cost of capital. The screener's depressed ROE/ROIC are write-down artifacts, not evidence of erosion.

**Secular threat: none of consequence.** Reinsurance faces no structural displacement tail. If anything, the secular wind is favorable — climate volatility, geopolitics, and cyber are *raising* demand for risk transfer, as management argued repeatedly. The cheapness here is a fear-print from the 2024 write-down and small-cap-of-the-cohort discount, not a structurally-shrinking base.

# SCOR SE (SCR.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*Global reinsurer, Euronext Paris. Price EUR 31.88 (2026-07-10), market cap ~EUR 5.7B, ~179M shares. Eight quarters of calls, Q4 2024 (2025-03-05) through Q4 2025 (2026-03-04), cross-checked against the screener financials and two dated post-transcript facts verified live: Q1 2026 results (2026-05-06) and the Covéa arbitration award (2026-06-25).*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

The story across these eight quarters is a clean, linear **recovery-and-rehabilitation arc**, and management stayed remarkably on-message throughout. The opening frame (Q4 2024) was damage control: 2024 was "a very challenging year," gutted by a Life & Health (L&H) assumption review that took full-year net income to essentially zero (EUR 4M) and knocked 29 points off the solvency ratio. The narrative even then was, "look through the one-off — underlying return on equity was 14.9%, not 0.2%." From there the emphasis shifted quarter by quarter from *defending the balance sheet* to *demonstrating consistent delivery*: Q1 2025 an 18.3% ROE, Q2 2025 20.1%, Q3 2025 19.5% nine-month, and Q4 2025 a full-year record net income of EUR 846M and a 19.1% ROE — "the highest level in SCOR's history."

The load-bearing pillars never changed: (1) an excellent P&C book run to a combined ratio comfortably below the 87% "Forward 2026" target (a combined ratio under 100% means the underwriting itself is profitable before investment income), with management *deliberately over-reserving* — "building buffers opportunistically" — every quarter; (2) an L&H book being nursed back to health under a three-step plan and a new divisional CEO; and (3) a high-quality, mostly fixed-income investment portfolio whose income keeps rising because reinvestment rates (~4.3%) sit above the running yield (~3.5%). Growth was quietly *dropped* as a headline: by Q3 2025 management explicitly recast the old "4–6% P&C revenue CAGR" as "an outcome, not an objective," and revenue actually shrank (down ~5.4% in 2025), replaced by a discipline-over-growth message as the reinsurance pricing cycle softened past its peak.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The financials say | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Highest net income in SCOR's history" (Q4 2025) | Net income EUR 846–851M in 2025 vs EUR 4M (2024), –1.38B (2022) | **Matches.** Genuine record — but off a trough, and 2025 was a benign-catastrophe year (nat-cat ratio 6.8% vs 10% budget) |
| P&C "excellent," combined ratio well below 87% | Combined ratio ran 80–85% through 2025; Q1 2026 at 80.2% | **Matches, with a caveat** — the reported ratio is flattered by low cats and by buffer-building that management can flex; normalized it is nearer 87% |
| ROE "well above target" | FY2025 ROE 19.1%; Q1 2026 21.7% | **Matches.** But note ROE was 0.2% (2024) and 2.3% (screener trailing) — the multi-year record is violently volatile |
| "Resilient, predictable dividend"; ratchet floor | Dividend raised to EUR 1.90 (2025), up 5.6%, new floor; ~6% yield | **Matches.** Solvency 215% (YE25) → 220% (Q1 26) funds it |
| Balance sheet "resilient" | Solvency 210–220% throughout; RT1 debt 5.6x oversubscribed | **Matches.** This is the strongest, most consistently corroborated claim |
| Economic value per share "well above our share price" (Q4 2024) | EV per share ~EUR 48 (YE24) vs price ~EUR 32; EV +13.7% in 2025, +7.4% in Q1 2026 | **Matches directionally** — the stock does trade at a large discount to SCOR's own economic value (~0.6x) |

The single most important forensic point sits *outside* the transcript, in the screener's "LIVE CORRECTIONS" block, which asserts EUR 17.99B of "net cash… a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back." **This is a category error and must not be credited.** For a reinsurer, cash and investments (~EUR 20B+) are held *against* policyholder reserves and insurance-contract liabilities; they are not excess corporate cash you can add to equity value. Treating EUR 18B of encumbered investment float as a net-cash top-up would triple the company's apparent value out of thin air. The right lenses for SCOR are price-to-earnings, price-to-book, and price-to-economic-value — not an industrial-style net-cash bridge.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Rising, then plateauing at confident.** The tonal glide is unmistakable. Q4 2024 was apologetic and defensive ("following a very challenging year"). By Q2 2025 CEO Thierry Leger was "very satisfied," and by Q4 2025 the language was assured to the point of victory-lap ("we fully leveraged SCOR's Tier 1 franchise"). Importantly, management resisted the temptation to over-claim on the one genuinely fragile area — L&H — repeatedly saying it was "premature to claim victory" (Q4 2025) and that experience trends need "at least 2 years" of data. That restraint is a credibility positive: they are confident on P&C and capital, appropriately hedged on L&H. The register also shifted from offensive (growth) to a mix of *disciplined defense* (cycle management, "we have no growth targets," walking away from soft U.S. casualty) — the correct posture for a reinsurer heading into a softening market.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**High.** The screener shows an 86% earnings-beat rate (6 of 7 quarters), and the qualitative track record corroborates it: the Forward 2026 P&C reserve-buffer target (EUR 300M) was hit "two years ahead of plan"; the L&H new-business target of ~EUR 400M came in at EUR 464M (2025); the EUR 170M cost-savings goal was delivered a year early; and full-year EV growth (13.7%) beat the 9% target. There is a visible **sandbagging pattern** — management holds the 87% combined-ratio guide while printing 80–85%, and explicitly banks prudence to release later ("we take the bad news upfront… and release the good news later," Q3 2025). That is conservative and shareholder-friendly, but it also means the *reported* numbers overstate the run-rate: strip the buffers and the underlying combined ratio is closer to the 87% guide than the 80% print. Reliability: **High**, with the honest asterisk that the earnings quality is deliberately understated, which cuts both ways for a valuation.

Three themes recur. First, **the Covéa arbitration** — Michael Huttner (Berenberg) and James Shuck pressed on it repeatedly; management deflected under confidentiality ("no comment on the P&L cover") and guided the decision to "the beginning of 2026." Second, **FX drag on solvency** — analysts (James Shuck) openly struggled to reconcile the small disclosed FX sensitivity with the large actual Q2 2025 solvency hit; management conceded its sensitivity model was still being "refined… by the end of the year," a genuine soft spot. 🟢 Deliberate over-reserving builds a cushion for a bad cat year or a soft market — real downside protection.

🔴 A residual, unquantified legal tail: former chairman Denis Kessler's estate/association remains under a separate French examination (management stresses "no direct implication of SCOR").

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

The terminology migrated from *growth* to *capital allocation discipline* — "no growth targets," "leave no stone unturned to find profitable opportunities," "we're prepared to reduce capacity or redeploy capital." The buffer language is the tell: management is quietly running an earnings-smoothing reserve, which is why the headline combined ratio (80%) and the normalized one (~87%) diverge. On the L&H side the mix is being re-pointed toward longevity and financial-solutions (less capital-intensive, higher-margin) and away from mortality protection — a slower, lower-visibility earnings stream. And the tax narrative (repatriating profit to France, redomiciling the Irish retro platform to Paris) is a multi-year effective-tax-rate story now converging to ~28%, a modest structural earnings tailwind that rarely gets priced.

The low multiple is a quality-and-cycle discount, not a melting terminal-value base — cheapness here is a mild mispricing, not a value trap, but also not a coiled spring.

bull_thesis:
SCOR is one of five large global reinsurers — a company that sells insurance to insurance companies — and it trades at about 0.68 times its own published measure of what it is worth. That measure, which SCOR calls economic value, stood at 8.5 billion euros or 48 euros per share at the end of 2025, and it grew 13.7% during the year against a 9% target. The shares change hands at 32.62 euros (Euronext Paris, live quote 17 July 2026). The bull case is that this gap is stale memory being priced as if it were permanent damage.

The memory is specific and three-fold: a 1.38 billion euro loss in 2022, a 2024 re-examination of the life book's actuarial assumptions that pushed 2024 return on equity — profit divided by shareholders' money — down to 0.2%, and a four-year arbitration fight with the French insurer Covea. Every one of those is now behind the company. The arbitration resolved on 25 June 2026: the tribunal confirmed the disputed treaties are valid and will keep running, awarded Covea 488.3 million dollars of compensation, and SCOR's own disclosure puts the net hit to its second-quarter 2026 results at about 50 million euros after existing provisions, with no impact on solvency or liquidity. A four-year overhang cost roughly three weeks of earnings.

What replaced the memory is five consecutive clean quarters and a management team that keeps refusing to take credit for them. Full-year 2025 net income was 851 million euros, the highest in SCOR's history, at a 19.1% return on equity against a plan assumption of 12%. The property and casualty combined ratio — claims plus expenses as a share of premium, where under 100% means the underwriting itself made money — came in at 82.3% against a guide of 'below 87%', and Q1 2026 delivered 80.2% with 225 million euros of net income and a 21.7% return on equity. Management has beaten that combined-ratio guide by four to seven points for two years and has flatly refused to raise it: asked directly in Q1 2025 whether they would lower the target, the P&C chief said 'we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence that we'll be able to meet a combined ratio below 87%.'

Crucially, the reported numbers understate the truth rather than flatter it. Management has been deliberately over-reserving: a 300 million euro buffer target set for end-2026 was exceeded within one year ('we have achieved significantly more buffer building in one year than we had planned over three years', Q4 2024), the prudence added in the first nine months of 2025 equalled the whole of 2024, and another 300 million euros went in during Q1 2026. The CFO described the mechanic plainly in Q3 2025: 'we tend to take the bad news upfront... and we release the good news later.' For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, this is the behaviour you want, and it means the 82.3% ratio contains, in management's words, 'a couple of points' of hidden margin.

The balance sheet did all of this while getting stronger, not weaker. Solvency — the regulatory cushion, where 100% is the legal minimum — went 210% at end-2024, 215% at end-2025, and 220% at 31 March 2026, which is the top of SCOR's own stated 185-220% optimal range. It absorbed a 140 million euro Los Angeles wildfire loss, the life review and the Covea award along the way. That leaves genuine surplus capital, and SCOR's capital framework explicitly allows buybacks or special dividends on top of the regular one. The regular dividend is 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management states the ratchet policy makes it a floor: a 5.8% yield while you wait.

Two further levers sit unmodelled. First, the interest-rate environment is a tailwind that needs no help from the Federal Reserve — the opposite of most value stories. SCOR runs a short-duration, high-quality bond portfolio (average rating A-) and reinvests maturing bonds at higher yields than the ones rolling off: 4.3% reinvestment against a 3.5% running yield as of Q1 2025. Every year that rates stay high, investment income mechanically rises. Second, credit quality is checkable and clean: total exposure to the First Brands and Tricolor failures was 0.2 million euros — 'it's nothing' — and zero exposure to French sovereign debt. In a market where private-credit stress is the live crack, that matters.

Finally, ratings. SCOR's rating gates its growth, and management framed the asymmetry honestly in Q4 2025: 'when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow our market share.' One of five agencies has already moved to positive outlook, and the CEO expects 'others will follow in the next 12, 18 months'. An upgrade would convert the Tier-1 franchise — access to every insurer's reinsurance programme worldwide — into actual share gains.

What has to hold: reinsurance pricing must stay adequate rather than collapse (management's read is that the market is 'more competitive' but 'still risk adequate'); the life book must not need a second assumption review; and management must eventually choose to return the surplus capital rather than bury it in reserves forever.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that SCOR is a bad company. It is that you are buying peak-cycle earnings on a shrinking base at a price 3% below the 52-week high, after the event that was supposed to force the re-rating has already happened.

Start with the fact management said out loud and the market appears to be ignoring. Reinsurance earnings arrive on a delay: the profit reported today comes from contracts written years ago. The P&C chief executive spelled it out in Q2 2025: 'you have to remember also in the financials that you earn through the previous underwriting years and quarters. So as we have had very good underwriting years 23, 24, 25, those will continue to earn through in 25 and probably early 26.' Reinsurance prices peaked in 2023-24 and have been softening since. The 80.2% combined ratio printed in Q1 2026 is therefore an echo of the best pricing in a decade. The CEO himself warned the industry in Q3 2025 that 'as profits are up and the supply of capacity now exceeds demand... underwriting discipline is being tested', and explained the mechanism that guarantees it gets worse: 'what's ultimately competing in our market is capital availability, and the capital is going up because we create a lot of capital these days.' Good years manufacture the capital that ruins the next ones. Anyone underwriting 21% return on equity as the run-rate is extrapolating the top.

Second, the base is genuinely shrinking. Group revenue fell 5.4% in 2025 and has compounded at -3.4% over three years. P&C revenue fell 4.4% to about 7.3 billion euros; life and health fell 4.8% to about 8.1 billion. Book value per share has compounded at -7.9% over five years. Management calls the shrinkage discipline — they walked away from US casualty at every renewal since January 2024 and stopped writing single-risk US casualty out of London and Paris — and that defence is largely fair. But the Forward 2026 plan promised 4-6% annual P&C revenue growth, and when an analyst asked in Q3 2025 whether they had abandoned it, the answer was a reclassification rather than a withdrawal: 'the 4% to 6% is more an outcome than an objective.' A shrinking company earning peak margins is a company whose earnings have two ways to fall and one narrow way to rise.

Third, the down-leg will be deliberately blurred and you will not be able to measure it. The reserve buffers are an explicit smoothing tool and their size has never been disclosed — analysts asked repeatedly and got 'a couple of points' and 'significantly above the 300 million euro target'. Asked directly whether the buffers would be used to cushion the soft market, the CFO said 'probably it's when the P&C cycle will be really soft, not before', and the CEO added 'it probably needs a combination of a soft market and a large claim.' So the plan is stated: when the cycle turns, reported earnings will be topped up from an undisclosed reserve. That is prudent management and terrible transparency. Reported combined ratios in 2027-28 will be partly manufactured, and no outsider will be able to decompose them.

Fourth, the catalyst is spent. The Covea arbitration — the item analysts asked about on every single call, and the one the company would not discuss ('No comment on this one', Q2 2025) — resolved on 25 June 2026, and it resolved against SCOR: the tribunal awarded the counterparty 488.3 million dollars. Provisions absorbed most of it, which is a credit to the balance sheet, but it is still a loss, and the uncertainty premium it carried has now been released into a share price sitting near its high. Everything left is soft and undated: a possible rating upgrade the CEO himself will only place at 'the next 12, 18 months' and which is an agency's decision, not SCOR's; a new strategic plan whose date is not yet public; and a buyback that has been made possible by 220% solvency but has not been announced. Management's revealed preference across five straight calls has been buffers over buybacks. Betting on capital return here is betting against their own demonstrated behaviour.

Fifth, the market already knows. This is not a thinly-covered name: roughly 15-20 sell-side houses cover it, and their average 12-month target of about 33.9-34.5 euros (web-sourced, mid-2026) sits within a few percent of the 32.62 euro price, with 8 buys and 7 holds. The shares are 8% above their 200-day average and 84% up the 52-week range. There is no forced selling, no activist, no orphaned stub, no analyst blind spot to arbitrage — just a fairly-followed reinsurer that has recovered and been noticed.

Sixth, the specific tail risks are real and dated to nothing. The 2024 life review took 29 percentage points of solvency and a year of earnings out of nowhere, and management explicitly refuses to declare it settled: 'it typically takes at least 2 years before trends can be properly assessed. With 4 quarters of data under IFRS, it remains premature to claim for any victory' (Q4 2025). A second review is a live possibility. The natural-catastrophe budget is 10% of premium and 2026 has run at 4.2% through Q1 — the Atlantic hurricane season has not happened yet. There is an open criminal examination touching former chairman Denis Kessler that management will only answer with confidentiality boilerplate. And the chief financial officer who architected the entire balance-sheet repair left the company at the end of Q4 2025.

What confirms the bear: a heavy catastrophe quarter reported on 30 October 2026, a 1 January 2027 renewal print showing rates down and volume flat, or any language shift from 'building' buffers to 'using' them — the CFO's own signal that the cycle has turned. On soft-market earnings of roughly 3.90 euros per share and a 6.5 times multiple, these shares are worth about 25 euros; with a second life-reserve event, less.

First, the screener-visible numbers on this company are actively misleading, and any model built on them is broken. The input carries '17.99 billion euros of NET CASH' described as 'a genuine sum-of-the-parts add-back' — roughly 100 euros a share on a 32.62 euro stock. It carries a 197.30 discounted-cash-flow fair value for a business whose cash flow is float. Anyone screening this name mechanically is either wildly bullish or wildly bearish for reasons that have nothing to do with SCOR.

Second, and more substantively: the market is anchored on SCOR's 2022-24 record and has not fully repriced the balance sheet that emerged. Solvency went 210% to 215% to 220% while absorbing a 140 million euro wildfire, a 348 million euro life review and a 488 million dollar arbitration award. Economic value grew 13.7% against a 9% target. The shares still trade at 0.68 times that economic value and about a third below European peers on book. Some of that discount is memory, not analysis.

But here is where the arbitrage runs out, and it is decisive. This is not a thinly-covered name — roughly 15 to 20 sell-side houses follow it, 8 buys and 7 holds, no sells, with an average 12-month target of about 33.9 to 34.5 euros (web-sourced, mid-2026). The price is 32.62. The street's target IS the price. There is no analyst blind spot left to arbitrage: they have seen the five clean quarters, they have marked the shares up 8% above the 200-day and to 84% of the 52-week range, and the Covea resolution three weeks ago removed the last thing they were discounting for.

The genuine remaining disagreement is one the market is arguably right about and the bulls are wrong. Consensus forward earnings growth of +6.9% implicitly assumes the current combined ratio is roughly sustainable. Management has told us, repeatedly and unprompted, that it is not the run-rate — the P&C chief in Q2 2025: 'we've had very good underwriting years 23, 24, 25, those will continue to earn through in 25 and probably early 26'; the CEO in Q3 2025: 'supply of capacity now exceeds demand... underwriting discipline is being tested.' The 80.2% ratio printed in Q1 2026 is an echo of peak pricing. If anything the street's +6.9% is too generous for 2027, not too stingy.

So: the market's error on this name has largely been corrected, and the residual error may point the wrong way. What remains is a fair-to-cheap price on a good business at a cyclical high — which is a valuation observation, not an expectations arbitrage.

positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical washout available here, and that absence is itself the finding.

This is a 5.8-billion-euro French reinsurer with a stable, income-oriented, largely institutional shareholder base and no forced-selling machinery attached to it: no index-orphan stub, no spin-off distribution, no post-lock-up overhang, no activist campaign, no regulator-ordered divestiture, no deal that could break. The practical read: the entry you want here will be handed to you by weather or by an actuary, not by a forced seller. Wait for it rather than manufacture a reason to pay 32.62 today. And note the mirror image of this — the same absence of forced flow that denies you a cheap entry also means there is no crowded position to be caught in. Nobody is over-owning this name.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good company at a fair-to-cheap price whose moment has just passed, and the discipline here is to say so rather than to reach.

What the work established. SCOR's repair is real and management's credibility is earned, not asserted. Across five consecutive calls every checkable claim came in at or above the promise: the '728 million euro clean base' the CFO staked his word on in Q4 2024 ('It's adjusted of everything. So it's clean and it's a good base for your estimates') became 851 million euros in 2025, the highest in the company's history; a 'below 87%' combined ratio guide delivered 82.3%; a 9% economic-value growth target delivered 13.7%; a 400 million euro life result delivered 450 million; a three-year cost programme delivered in two. And the reported numbers understate rather than flatter: management has been over-reserving deliberately and refuses to raise its own bar even after beating it by seven points. For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, that is exactly right.

The valuation gap is genuine. The shares change hands at 0.68 times SCOR's own published 48 euro economic value per share, about 6.7 times trailing earnings against Munich Re at 9.8 and Swiss Re at 14.5, and 1.32 times book against European peers at 1.9 to 2.2. The sum-of-the-parts build — P&C at 34.10, life and health at 10.40, corporate and debt at minus 9.00, a quarter of the surplus capital at 2.50 — lands at 38 euros, and the earnings and economic-value cross-checks agree.

Why that is not enough today. Three things, and they compound.

First, the catalyst is spent. Covea — the question analysts asked on every single call and management refused to answer — resolved on 25 June 2026, three weeks ago, and cost roughly three weeks of earnings. That is a fine outcome and it is now in the price: the shares sit 3% below their 52-week high, 8% above the 200-day, at 84% of the 52-week range. Everything left is soft and undated: a rating upgrade the CEO places at '12, 18 months' and does not control, a strategic plan with no announced date, a buyback contradicted by five straight quarters of choosing buffers instead.

Second, the earnings are the peak and management said so. The P&C chief in Q2 2025: 'we've had very good underwriting years 23, 24, 25, those will continue to earn through in 25 and probably early 26.' The CEO in Q3 2025: 'supply of capacity now exceeds demand... underwriting discipline is being tested.' Prices have softened since 2024; the reported ratio will not feel it until 2027. And when it does, the down-leg will be smoothed from an undisclosed reserve — management has stated the plan ('probably it's when the P&C cycle will be really soft') and has never disclosed the size. bull_thesis:
SCOR is one of five large global reinsurers — a company that sells insurance to insurance companies — and it trades at about 0.68 times its own published measure of what it is worth. That measure, which SCOR calls economic value, stood at 8.5 billion euros or 48 euros per share at the end of 2025, and it grew 13.7% during the year against a 9% target. The shares change hands at 32.62 euros (Euronext Paris, live quote 17 July 2026). The bull case is that this gap is stale memory being priced as if it were permanent damage.

The memory is specific and three-fold: a 1.38 billion euro loss in 2022, a 2024 re-examination of the life book's actuarial assumptions that pushed 2024 return on equity — profit divided by shareholders' money — down to 0.2%, and a four-year arbitration fight with the French insurer Covea. Every one of those is now behind the company. The arbitration resolved on 25 June 2026: the tribunal confirmed the disputed treaties are valid and will keep running, awarded Covea 488.3 million dollars of compensation, and SCOR's own disclosure puts the net hit to its second-quarter 2026 results at about 50 million euros after existing provisions, with no impact on solvency or liquidity. A four-year overhang cost roughly three weeks of earnings.

What replaced the memory is five consecutive clean quarters and a management team that keeps refusing to take credit for them. Full-year 2025 net income was 851 million euros, the highest in SCOR's history, at a 19.1% return on equity against a plan assumption of 12%. The property and casualty combined ratio — claims plus expenses as a share of premium, where under 100% means the underwriting itself made money — came in at 82.3% against a guide of 'below 87%', and Q1 2026 delivered 80.2% with 225 million euros of net income and a 21.7% return on equity. Management has beaten that combined-ratio guide by four to seven points for two years and has flatly refused to raise it: asked directly in Q1 2025 whether they would lower the target, the P&C chief said 'we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence that we'll be able to meet a combined ratio below 87%.'

Crucially, the reported numbers understate the truth rather than flatter it. Management has been deliberately over-reserving: a 300 million euro buffer target set for end-2026 was exceeded within one year ('we have achieved significantly more buffer building in one year than we had planned over three years', Q4 2024), the prudence added in the first nine months of 2025 equalled the whole of 2024, and another 300 million euros went in during Q1 2026. The CFO described the mechanic plainly in Q3 2025: 'we tend to take the bad news upfront... and we release the good news later.' For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, this is the behaviour you want, and it means the 82.3% ratio contains, in management's words, 'a couple of points' of hidden margin.

The balance sheet did all of this while getting stronger, not weaker. Solvency — the regulatory cushion, where 100% is the legal minimum — went 210% at end-2024, 215% at end-2025, and 220% at 31 March 2026, which is the top of SCOR's own stated 185-220% optimal range. It absorbed a 140 million euro Los Angeles wildfire loss, the life review and the Covea award along the way. That leaves genuine surplus capital, and SCOR's capital framework explicitly allows buybacks or special dividends on top of the regular one. The regular dividend is 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management states the ratchet policy makes it a floor: a 5.8% yield while you wait.

Two further levers sit unmodelled. First, the interest-rate environment is a tailwind that needs no help from the Federal Reserve — the opposite of most value stories. SCOR runs a short-duration, high-quality bond portfolio (average rating A-) and reinvests maturing bonds at higher yields than the ones rolling off: 4.3% reinvestment against a 3.5% running yield as of Q1 2025. Every year that rates stay high, investment income mechanically rises. Second, credit quality is checkable and clean: total exposure to the First Brands and Tricolor failures was 0.2 million euros — 'it's nothing' — and zero exposure to French sovereign debt. In a market where private-credit stress is the live crack, that matters.

Finally, ratings. SCOR's rating gates its growth, and management framed the asymmetry honestly in Q4 2025: 'when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow our market share.' One of five agencies has already moved to positive outlook, and the CEO expects 'others will follow in the next 12, 18 months'. An upgrade would convert the Tier-1 franchise — access to every insurer's reinsurance programme worldwide — into actual share gains.

What has to hold: reinsurance pricing must stay adequate rather than collapse (management's read is that the market is 'more competitive' but 'still risk adequate'); the life book must not need a second assumption review; and management must eventually choose to return the surplus capital rather than bury it in reserves forever.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that SCOR is a bad company. It is that you are buying peak-cycle earnings on a shrinking base at a price 3% below the 52-week high, after the event that was supposed to force the re-rating has already happened.

Start with the fact management said out loud and the market appears to be ignoring. Reinsurance earnings arrive on a delay: the profit reported today comes from contracts written years ago. Good years manufacture the capital that ruins the next ones. Anyone underwriting 21% return on equity as the run-rate is extrapolating the top.

Second, the base is genuinely shrinking. Group revenue fell 5.4% in 2025 and has compounded at -3.4% over three years. With 4 quarters of data under IFRS, it remains premature to claim for any victory' (Q4 2025). A second review is a live possibility. The regime read makes this sharper, not softer. bull_thesis:
SCOR is one of five large global reinsurers — a company that sells insurance to insurance companies — and it trades at about 0.68 times its own published measure of what it is worth. That measure, which SCOR calls economic value, stood at 8.5 billion euros or 48 euros per share at the end of 2025, and it grew 13.7% during the year against a 9% target. The shares change hands at 32.62 euros (Euronext Paris, live quote 17 July 2026). The bull case is that this gap is stale memory being priced as if it were permanent damage.

The memory is specific and three-fold: a 1.38 billion euro loss in 2022, a 2024 re-examination of the life book's actuarial assumptions that pushed 2024 return on equity — profit divided by shareholders' money — down to 0.2%, and a four-year arbitration fight with the French insurer Covea. Every one of those is now behind the company. The arbitration resolved on 25 June 2026: the tribunal confirmed the disputed treaties are valid and will keep running, awarded Covea 488.3 million dollars of compensation, and SCOR's own disclosure puts the net hit to its second-quarter 2026 results at about 50 million euros after existing provisions, with no impact on solvency or liquidity. A four-year overhang cost roughly three weeks of earnings.

What replaced the memory is five consecutive clean quarters and a management team that keeps refusing to take credit for them. Full-year 2025 net income was 851 million euros, the highest in SCOR's history, at a 19.1% return on equity against a plan assumption of 12%. The property and casualty combined ratio — claims plus expenses as a share of premium, where under 100% means the underwriting itself made money — came in at 82.3% against a guide of 'below 87%', and Q1 2026 delivered 80.2% with 225 million euros of net income and a 21.7% return on equity. Management has beaten that combined-ratio guide by four to seven points for two years and has flatly refused to raise it: asked directly in Q1 2025 whether they would lower the target, the P&C chief said 'we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence that we'll be able to meet a combined ratio below 87%.'

Crucially, the reported numbers understate the truth rather than flatter it. Management has been deliberately over-reserving: a 300 million euro buffer target set for end-2026 was exceeded within one year ('we have achieved significantly more buffer building in one year than we had planned over three years', Q4 2024), the prudence added in the first nine months of 2025 equalled the whole of 2024, and another 300 million euros went in during Q1 2026. The CFO described the mechanic plainly in Q3 2025: 'we tend to take the bad news upfront... and we release the good news later.' For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, this is the behaviour you want, and it means the 82.3% ratio contains, in management's words, 'a couple of points' of hidden margin.

The balance sheet did all of this while getting stronger, not weaker. Solvency — the regulatory cushion, where 100% is the legal minimum — went 210% at end-2024, 215% at end-2025, and 220% at 31 March 2026, which is the top of SCOR's own stated 185-220% optimal range. It absorbed a 140 million euro Los Angeles wildfire loss, the life review and the Covea award along the way. That leaves genuine surplus capital, and SCOR's capital framework explicitly allows buybacks or special dividends on top of the regular one. The regular dividend is 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management states the ratchet policy makes it a floor: a 5.8% yield while you wait.

SCOR runs a short-duration, high-quality bond portfolio (average rating A-) and reinvests maturing bonds at higher yields than the ones rolling off: 4.3% reinvestment against a 3.5% running yield as of Q1 2025. Every year that rates stay high, investment income mechanically rises. Second, credit quality is checkable and clean: total exposure to the First Brands and Tricolor failures was 0.2 million euros — 'it's nothing' — and zero exposure to French sovereign debt. In a market where private-credit stress is the live crack, that matters.

Finally, ratings. SCOR's rating gates its growth, and management framed the asymmetry honestly in Q4 2025: 'when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow our market share.' One of five agencies has already moved to positive outlook, and the CEO expects 'others will follow in the next 12, 18 months'. An upgrade would convert the Tier-1 franchise — access to every insurer's reinsurance programme worldwide — into actual share gains.

What has to hold: reinsurance pricing must stay adequate rather than collapse (management's read is that the market is 'more competitive' but 'still risk adequate'); the life book must not need a second assumption review; and management must eventually choose to return the surplus capital rather than bury it in reserves forever.

positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical washout available here, and that absence is itself the finding.

This is a 5.8-billion-euro French reinsurer with a stable, income-oriented, largely institutional shareholder base and no forced-selling machinery attached to it: no index-orphan stub, no spin-off distribution, no post-lock-up overhang, no activist campaign, no regulator-ordered divestiture, no deal that could break. In the current regime the fattest lane is forced sellers and spin-offs — mechanical, price-insensitive, calendar-dated flow. SCOR offers none of it.

Worse, for anyone hoping the yield-focused base gets flushed out: the dividend is going the other way. SCOR raised it to 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management explicitly stated the ratchet policy makes that a new floor. The only realistic source of a flush is fundamental, not mechanical: a large catastrophe quarter or a second life-reserve surprise. Those would hit the shares hard — the 2024 review took them to roughly 19-20 euros — but they are events, not positioning. You cannot schedule them.

The practical read: the entry you want here will be handed to you by weather or by an actuary, not by a forced seller. Wait for it rather than manufacture a reason to pay 32.62 today. And note the mirror image of this — the same absence of forced flow that denies you a cheap entry also means there is no crowded position to be caught in. Nobody is over-owning this name.
moderator_conclusion:
This is a good company at a fair-to-cheap price whose moment has just passed, and the discipline here is to say so rather than to reach.

What the work established. SCOR's repair is real and management's credibility is earned, not asserted. The valuation gap is genuine. First, the catalyst is spent. Covea — the question analysts asked on every single call and management refused to answer — resolved on 25 June 2026, three weeks ago, and cost roughly three weeks of earnings. That is a fine outcome and it is now in the price: the shares sit 3% below their 52-week high, 8% above the 200-day, at 84% of the 52-week range. The regime read makes this sharper, not softer. The current tilt rewards hard-dated catalysts inside the window and structural special-situations in thin-coverage lanes, and penalises catalysts that have already fired or sit out of window. Two things do cut in SCOR's favour and deserve credit: the hawkish, higher-for-longer rate path is a genuine tailwind here rather than the rate-cut rescue this regime rightly punishes — SCOR reinvests short-duration bonds at 4.3% against a 3.5% running yield, so every year rates stay high the investment income mechanically rises. bull_thesis:
SCOR is one of five large global reinsurers — a company that sells insurance to insurance companies — and it trades at about 0.68 times its own published measure of what it is worth. That measure, which SCOR calls economic value, stood at 8.5 billion euros or 48 euros per share at the end of 2025, and it grew 13.7% during the year against a 9% target. The shares change hands at 32.62 euros (Euronext Paris, live quote 17 July 2026). The bull case is that this gap is stale memory being priced as if it were permanent damage.

The memory is specific and three-fold: a 1.38 billion euro loss in 2022, a 2024 re-examination of the life book's actuarial assumptions that pushed 2024 return on equity — profit divided by shareholders' money — down to 0.2%, and a four-year arbitration fight with the French insurer Covea. Every one of those is now behind the company. The arbitration resolved on 25 June 2026: the tribunal confirmed the disputed treaties are valid and will keep running, awarded Covea 488.3 million dollars of compensation, and SCOR's own disclosure puts the net hit to its second-quarter 2026 results at about 50 million euros after existing provisions, with no impact on solvency or liquidity. A four-year overhang cost roughly three weeks of earnings.

What replaced the memory is five consecutive clean quarters and a management team that keeps refusing to take credit for them. Full-year 2025 net income was 851 million euros, the highest in SCOR's history, at a 19.1% return on equity against a plan assumption of 12%. The property and casualty combined ratio — claims plus expenses as a share of premium, where under 100% means the underwriting itself made money — came in at 82.3% against a guide of 'below 87%', and Q1 2026 delivered 80.2% with 225 million euros of net income and a 21.7% return on equity. Management has beaten that combined-ratio guide by four to seven points for two years and has flatly refused to raise it: asked directly in Q1 2025 whether they would lower the target, the P&C chief said 'we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence that we'll be able to meet a combined ratio below 87%.'

Crucially, the reported numbers understate the truth rather than flatter it. Management has been deliberately over-reserving: a 300 million euro buffer target set for end-2026 was exceeded within one year ('we have achieved significantly more buffer building in one year than we had planned over three years', Q4 2024), the prudence added in the first nine months of 2025 equalled the whole of 2024, and another 300 million euros went in during Q1 2026. The CFO described the mechanic plainly in Q3 2025: 'we tend to take the bad news upfront... and we release the good news later.' For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, this is the behaviour you want, and it means the 82.3% ratio contains, in management's words, 'a couple of points' of hidden margin.

The balance sheet did all of this while getting stronger, not weaker. Solvency — the regulatory cushion, where 100% is the legal minimum — went 210% at end-2024, 215% at end-2025, and 220% at 31 March 2026, which is the top of SCOR's own stated 185-220% optimal range. It absorbed a 140 million euro Los Angeles wildfire loss, the life review and the Covea award along the way. That leaves genuine surplus capital, and SCOR's capital framework explicitly allows buybacks or special dividends on top of the regular one. The regular dividend is 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management states the ratchet policy makes it a floor: a 5.8% yield while you wait.

Two further levers sit unmodelled. First, the interest-rate environment is a tailwind that needs no help from the Federal Reserve — the opposite of most value stories. SCOR runs a short-duration, high-quality bond portfolio (average rating A-) and reinvests maturing bonds at higher yields than the ones rolling off: 4.3% reinvestment against a 3.5% running yield as of Q1 2025. Every year that rates stay high, investment income mechanically rises. Second, credit quality is checkable and clean: total exposure to the First Brands and Tricolor failures was 0.2 million euros — 'it's nothing' — and zero exposure to French sovereign debt. In a market where private-credit stress is the live crack, that matters.

Finally, ratings. SCOR's rating gates its growth, and management framed the asymmetry honestly in Q4 2025: 'when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow our market share.' One of five agencies has already moved to positive outlook, and the CEO expects 'others will follow in the next 12, 18 months'. An upgrade would convert the Tier-1 franchise — access to every insurer's reinsurance programme worldwide — into actual share gains.

What has to hold: reinsurance pricing must stay adequate rather than collapse (management's read is that the market is 'more competitive' but 'still risk adequate'); the life book must not need a second assumption review; and management must eventually choose to return the surplus capital rather than bury it in reserves forever.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that SCOR is a bad company. It is that you are buying peak-cycle earnings on a shrinking base at a price 3% below the 52-week high, after the event that was supposed to force the re-rating has already happened.

Start with the fact management said out loud and the market appears to be ignoring. Reinsurance earnings arrive on a delay: the profit reported today comes from contracts written years ago. The P&C chief executive spelled it out in Q2 2025: 'you have to remember also in the financials that you earn through the previous underwriting years and quarters. So as we have had very good underwriting years 23, 24, 25, those will continue to earn through in 25 and probably early 26.' Reinsurance prices peaked in 2023-24 and have been softening since. The 80.2% combined ratio printed in Q1 2026 is therefore an echo of the best pricing in a decade. The CEO himself warned the industry in Q3 2025 that 'as profits are up and the supply of capacity now exceeds demand... underwriting discipline is being tested', and explained the mechanism that guarantees it gets worse: 'what's ultimately competing in our market is capital availability, and the capital is going up because we create a lot of capital these days.' Good years manufacture the capital that ruins the next ones. Anyone underwriting 21% return on equity as the run-rate is extrapolating the top.

Second, the base is genuinely shrinking. Group revenue fell 5.4% in 2025 and has compounded at -3.4% over three years. P&C revenue fell 4.4% to about 7.3 billion euros; life and health fell 4.8% to about 8.1 billion. Book value per share has compounded at -7.9% over five years. Management calls the shrinkage discipline — they walked away from US casualty at every renewal since January 2024 and stopped writing single-risk US casualty out of London and Paris — and that defence is largely fair. But the Forward 2026 plan promised 4-6% annual P&C revenue growth, and when an analyst asked in Q3 2025 whether they had abandoned it, the answer was a reclassification rather than a withdrawal: 'the 4% to 6% is more an outcome than an objective.' A shrinking company earning peak margins is a company whose earnings have two ways to fall and one narrow way to rise.

Third, the down-leg will be deliberately blurred and you will not be able to measure it. The reserve buffers are an explicit smoothing tool and their size has never been disclosed — analysts asked repeatedly and got 'a couple of points' and 'significantly above the 300 million euro target'. Asked directly whether the buffers would be used to cushion the soft market, the CFO said 'probably it's when the P&C cycle will be really soft, not before', and the CEO added 'it probably needs a combination of a soft market and a large claim.' So the plan is stated: when the cycle turns, reported earnings will be topped up from an undisclosed reserve. That is prudent management and terrible transparency. Reported combined ratios in 2027-28 will be partly manufactured, and no outsider will be able to decompose them.

Fourth, the catalyst is spent. The Covea arbitration — the item analysts asked about on every single call, and the one the company would not discuss ('No comment on this one', Q2 2025) — resolved on 25 June 2026, and it resolved against SCOR: the tribunal awarded the counterparty 488.3 million dollars. Provisions absorbed most of it, which is a credit to the balance sheet, but it is still a loss, and the uncertainty premium it carried has now been released into a share price sitting near its high. Everything left is soft and undated: a possible rating upgrade the CEO himself will only place at 'the next 12, 18 months' and which is an agency's decision, not SCOR's; a new strategic plan whose date is not yet public; and a buyback that has been made possible by 220% solvency but has not been announced. Fifth, the market already knows. The shares are 8% above their 200-day average and 84% up the 52-week range. There is no forced selling, no activist, no orphaned stub, no analyst blind spot to arbitrage — just a fairly-followed reinsurer that has recovered and been noticed.

Sixth, the specific tail risks are real and dated to nothing. The 2024 life review took 29 percentage points of solvency and a year of earnings out of nowhere, and management explicitly refuses to declare it settled: 'it typically takes at least 2 years before trends can be properly assessed. With 4 quarters of data under IFRS, it remains premature to claim for any victory' (Q4 2025). A second review is a live possibility. The natural-catastrophe budget is 10% of premium and 2026 has run at 4.2% through Q1 — the Atlantic hurricane season has not happened yet. And the chief financial officer who architected the entire balance-sheet repair left the company at the end of Q4 2025.

What confirms the bear: a heavy catastrophe quarter reported on 30 October 2026, a 1 January 2027 renewal print showing rates down and volume flat, or any language shift from 'building' buffers to 'using' them — the CFO's own signal that the cycle has turned. On soft-market earnings of roughly 3.90 euros per share and a 6.5 times multiple, these shares are worth about 25 euros; with a second life-reserve event, less.

positioning_washout:

This is a 5.8-billion-euro French reinsurer with a stable, income-oriented, largely institutional shareholder base and no forced-selling machinery attached to it: no index-orphan stub, no spin-off distribution, no post-lock-up overhang, no activist campaign, no regulator-ordered divestiture, no deal that could break. The only realistic source of a flush is fundamental, not mechanical: a large catastrophe quarter or a second life-reserve surprise. Those would hit the shares hard — the 2024 review took them to roughly 19-20 euros — but they are events, not positioning. You cannot schedule them.

The practical read: the entry you want here will be handed to you by weather or by an actuary, not by a forced seller. Wait for it rather than manufacture a reason to pay 32.62 today. moderator_conclusion:

The regime read makes this sharper, not softer. The current tilt rewards hard-dated catalysts inside the window and structural special-situations in thin-coverage lanes, and penalises catalysts that have already fired or sit out of window. SCOR is the wrong shape on every count: no spin, no forced flow, no activist, no deal, and roughly 15 to 20 analysts covering it with an average target of 33.9 to 34.5 euros — the street's target IS the price. That is a hold, not a bargain: three. bull_thesis:
SCOR is one of five large global reinsurers — a company that sells insurance to insurance companies — and it trades at about 0.68 times its own published measure of what it is worth. That measure, which SCOR calls economic value, stood at 8.5 billion euros or 48 euros per share at the end of 2025, and it grew 13.7% during the year against a 9% target. The shares change hands at 32.62 euros (Euronext Paris, live quote 17 July 2026). The bull case is that this gap is stale memory being priced as if it were permanent damage.

The memory is specific and three-fold: a 1.38 billion euro loss in 2022, a 2024 re-examination of the life book's actuarial assumptions that pushed 2024 return on equity — profit divided by shareholders' money — down to 0.2%, and a four-year arbitration fight with the French insurer Covea. Every one of those is now behind the company. The arbitration resolved on 25 June 2026: the tribunal confirmed the disputed treaties are valid and will keep running, awarded Covea 488.3 million dollars of compensation, and SCOR's own disclosure puts the net hit to its second-quarter 2026 results at about 50 million euros after existing provisions, with no impact on solvency or liquidity. A four-year overhang cost roughly three weeks of earnings.

What replaced the memory is five consecutive clean quarters and a management team that keeps refusing to take credit for them. Full-year 2025 net income was 851 million euros, the highest in SCOR's history, at a 19.1% return on equity against a plan assumption of 12%. The property and casualty combined ratio — claims plus expenses as a share of premium, where under 100% means the underwriting itself made money — came in at 82.3% against a guide of 'below 87%', and Q1 2026 delivered 80.2% with 225 million euros of net income and a 21.7% return on equity. Management has beaten that combined-ratio guide by four to seven points for two years and has flatly refused to raise it: asked directly in Q1 2025 whether they would lower the target, the P&C chief said 'we don't intend to change our guidance, but we have high confidence that we'll be able to meet a combined ratio below 87%.'

Crucially, the reported numbers understate the truth rather than flatter it. Management has been deliberately over-reserving: a 300 million euro buffer target set for end-2026 was exceeded within one year ('we have achieved significantly more buffer building in one year than we had planned over three years', Q4 2024), the prudence added in the first nine months of 2025 equalled the whole of 2024, and another 300 million euros went in during Q1 2026. The CFO described the mechanic plainly in Q3 2025: 'we tend to take the bad news upfront... and we release the good news later.' For a company whose near-death experience was caused by under-reserving, this is the behaviour you want, and it means the 82.3% ratio contains, in management's words, 'a couple of points' of hidden margin.

The balance sheet did all of this while getting stronger, not weaker. Solvency — the regulatory cushion, where 100% is the legal minimum — went 210% at end-2024, 215% at end-2025, and 220% at 31 March 2026, which is the top of SCOR's own stated 185-220% optimal range. It absorbed a 140 million euro Los Angeles wildfire loss, the life review and the Covea award along the way. That leaves genuine surplus capital, and SCOR's capital framework explicitly allows buybacks or special dividends on top of the regular one. The regular dividend is 1.9 euros per share for 2025, up 5.6%, and management states the ratchet policy makes it a floor: a 5.8% yield while you wait.

Two further levers sit unmodelled. First, the interest-rate environment is a tailwind that needs no help from the Federal Reserve — the opposite of most value stories. SCOR runs a short-duration, high-quality bond portfolio (average rating A-) and reinvests maturing bonds at higher yields than the ones rolling off: 4.3% reinvestment against a 3.5% running yield as of Q1 2025. Every year that rates stay high, investment income mechanically rises. Second, credit quality is checkable and clean: total exposure to the First Brands and Tricolor failures was 0.2 million euros — 'it's nothing' — and zero exposure to French sovereign debt. In a market where private-credit stress is the live crack, that matters.

Finally, ratings. SCOR's rating gates its growth, and management framed the asymmetry honestly in Q4 2025: 'when it went down, we didn't really lose business, but now on the way up, we will count on it to grow our market share.' One of five agencies has already moved to positive outlook, and the CEO expects 'others will follow in the next 12, 18 months'. An upgrade would convert the Tier-1 franchise — access to every insurer's reinsurance programme worldwide — into actual share gains.

What has to hold: reinsurance pricing must stay adequate rather than collapse (management's read is that the market is 'more competitive' but 'still risk adequate'); the life book must not need a second assumption review; and management must eventually choose to return the surplus capital rather than bury it in reserves forever.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that SCOR is a bad company. It is that you are buying peak-cycle earnings on a shrinking base at a price 3% below the 52-week high, after the event that was supposed to force the re-rating has already happened.

Start with the fact management said out loud and the market appears to be ignoring. Reinsurance earnings arrive on a delay: the profit reported today comes from contracts written years ago. The P&C chief executive spelled it out in Q2 2025: 'you have to remember also in the financials that you earn through the previous underwriting years and quarters. So as we have had very good underwriting years 23, 24, 25, those will continue to earn through in 25 and probably early 26.' Reinsurance prices peaked in 2023-24 and have been softening since. The 80.2% combined ratio printed in Q1 2026 is therefore an echo of the best pricing in a decade. The CEO himself warned the industry in Q3 2025 that 'as profits are up and the supply of capacity now exceeds demand... underwriting discipline is being tested', and explained the mechanism that guarantees it gets worse: 'what's ultimately competing in our market is capital availability, and the capital is going up because we create a lot of capital these days.' Good years manufacture the capital that ruins the next ones. Anyone underwriting 21% return on equity as the run-rate is extrapolating the top.

Second, the base is genuinely shrinking. Group revenue fell 5.4% in 2025 and has compounded at -3.4% over three years. P&C revenue fell 4.4% to about 7.3 billion euros; life and health fell 4.8% to about 8.1 billion. Book value per share has compounded at -7.9% over five years. Management calls the shrinkage discipline — they walked away from US casualty at every renewal since January 2024 and stopped writing single-risk US casualty out of London and Paris — and that defence is largely fair. But the Forward 2026 plan promised 4-6% annual P&C revenue growth, and when an analyst asked in Q3 2025 whether they had abandoned it, the answer was a reclassification rather than a withdrawal: 'the 4% to 6% is more an outcome than an objective.' A shrinking company earning peak margins is a company whose earnings have two ways to fall and one narrow way to rise.

Third, the down-leg will be deliberately blurred and you will not be able to measure it. The reserve buffers are an explicit smoothing tool and their size has never been disclosed — analysts asked repeatedly and got 'a couple of points' and 'significantly above the 300 million euro target'. Asked directly whether the buffers would be used to cushion the soft market, the CFO said 'probably it's when the P&C cycle will be really soft, not before', and the CEO added 'it probably needs a combination of a soft market and a large claim.' So the plan is stated: when the cycle turns, reported earnings will be topped up from an undisclosed reserve. That is prudent management and terrible transparency. Reported combined ratios in 2027-28 will be partly manufactured, and no outsider will be able to decompose them.

The Covea arbitration — the item analysts asked about on every single call, and the one the company would not discuss ('No comment on this one', Q2 2025) — resolved on 25 June 2026, and it resolved against SCOR: the tribunal awarded the counterparty 488.3 million dollars. Provisions absorbed most of it, which is a credit to the balance sheet, but it is still a loss, and the uncertainty premium it carried has now been released into a share price sitting near its high. Everything left is soft and undated: a possible rating upgrade the CEO himself will only place at 'the next 12, 18 months' and which is an agency's decision, not SCOR's; a new strategic plan whose date is not yet public; and a buyback that has been made possible by 220% solvency but has not been announced. Management's revealed preference across five straight calls has been buffers over buybacks. Betting on capital return here is betting against their own demonstrated behaviour.

Fifth, the market already knows. This is not a thinly-covered name: roughly 15-20 sell-side houses cover it, and their average 12-month target of about 33.9-34.5 euros (web-sourced, mid-2026) sits within a few percent of the 32.62 euro price, with 8 buys and 7 holds. The shares are 8% above their 200-day average and 84% up the 52-week range. There is no forced selling, no activist, no orphaned stub, no analyst blind spot to arbitrage — just a fairly-followed reinsurer that has recovered and been noticed.

Sixth, the specific tail risks are real and dated to nothing. The 2024 life review took 29 percentage points of solvency and a year of earnings out of nowhere, and management explicitly refuses to declare it settled: 'it typically takes at least 2 years before trends can be properly assessed. With 4 quarters of data under IFRS, it remains premature to claim for any victory' (Q4 2025). A second review is a live possibility. The natural-catastrophe budget is 10% of premium and 2026 has run at 4.2% through Q1 — the Atlantic hurricane season has not happened yet. There is an open criminal examination touching former chairman Denis Kessler that management will only answer with confidentiality boilerplate. And the chief financial officer who architected the entire balance-sheet repair left the company at the end of Q4 2025.

What confirms the bear: a heavy catastrophe quarter reported on 30 October 2026, a 1 January 2027 renewal print showing rates down and volume flat, or any language shift from 'building' buffers to 'using' them — the CFO's own signal that the cycle has turned. On soft-market earnings of roughly 3.90 euros per share and a 6.5 times multiple, these shares are worth about 25 euros; with a second life-reserve event, less.
